analysis.one_liner: Speeds up black lung disability payments to miners by making the federal fund pay when companies delay.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have sped up black lung benefit payments to sick miners, died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Miners with black lung disease are supposed to get monthly federal benefits, but if no one has determined which coal company is responsible for paying, the checks wait until that fight is settled — sometimes years. This bill would have required the Labor Department to start paying benefits out of the federal Black Lung Disability Trust Fund within 60 days of an award, and then collect the money back from the coal company later if the company is found responsible. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Miners awarded black lung benefits and their surviving families. Instead of waiting years while companies and the government argue over which coal operator is responsible, they would start receiving monthly checks within 60 days, with the government recouping the cost from the responsible company afterward. Their communities in coal country also benefit, since disabled miners would not fall into debt while claims sit in litigation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sick coal miners and their families

how_it_helps.text: If the government has not figured out which company owes a miner's black lung benefits within 60 days of the award, the Department of Labor must start paying the benefits out of the federal black lung fund right away.
The miner no longer waits, sometimes for years, while companies argue over responsibility; if a coal company is later found responsible, it must repay the fund rather than the bill erasing that debt.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Black Lung Disability Trust Fund fronts the money during liability disputes, though it can recover from the responsible coal company later. The trust fund is financed by an excise tax on coal, so the coal industry ultimately bears the cost either way — but under this bill the government, not the miner, carries the wait.
analysis.who_pays_short: The federal black lung trust fund, recouped from operators

drawbacks.text: The government's black lung trust fund would have to front the money during disputes, adding cash-flow pressure to a fund that is already financially strained and financed by an excise tax on coal production.

Shifting the timing of payments does not shorten the underlying legal fights over who is liable; coal operators still contest claims, and the bill addresses the delay in benefits, not the delay in the decisions themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: sick miners and widows would get money months or years sooner instead of waiting out disputes between coal companies and the Labor Department. The cost is cash-flow pressure on the federal Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which is already in debt and funded by a coal excise tax; the bill wisely keeps coal companies on the hook for repayment if they are later found liable, so the main risk is timing, not a lasting shift of costs onto taxpayers. The trade-off is modest and, for the people involved, urgent.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees in December 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote before the two-year session of Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 6, 2023 by Rep. Harold Rogers of Kentucky, a Republican, with three other cosponsors.
Referred to two committees, Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means, the day it was introduced; no further action was taken.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators keep the status quo: they can contest liability for years while sick miners and their families wait for benefits, with no pressure from a fast-payment rule.

for.name: Rep. Sanford Bishop
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: House Republican leadership and committee chairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration or a floor vote, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from coal-country and mining-district members of both parties, but with only four cosponsors it never generated a recorded vote that would show where the parties stood.

industries.note: Companies found responsible for a miner's black lung benefits would still owe the money but would lose the benefit of having the miner wait years while liability disputes drag on; the interest-free delay in paying for their workers' disease would effectively end.

industries.industry: Black Lung Disability Trust Fund (federal trust fund financed by coal excise taxes)
industries.note: The fund would pay benefits sooner and wait longer for reimbursement from operators, straining its cash flow in the short term, while keeping repayment liability on the companies preserves its long-term finances.
